Postponed Marriage to Beautiful American Girl Takes Place in London.

Prince Albert Radziwill and Miss Dorothy Deacon, the beautiful daughter of the late Mr. Edward Parker Deacon, of Boston, and of Mrs. Baldwin, of Paris and New York, were quietly married yesterday morning at St. Mary's Roman Catholic Church, Cadogan-street, W.

Only a few invited guests were present at the ceremony, and admission was by ticket only. Last Wednesday a large number of people assembled at the church for the wedding, but neither bride nor bridegroom arrived, the explanation of the postponement being that certain papers had not arrived from Russia.

The Prince drove up to the church yesterday in a taxicab with his best man, M. de Halpent, shortly after eleven o'clock. Lord Grey de Ruthyn accompanied the bride to the church from a Jermyn-street hotel, where she has been staying with her mother, and gave her away.

Only eighteen years old, the bride looked very lovely in a dress of white point de Paris laid drawn into a deep hem of white satin. Her white straw hat was draped with clouds of white tulle and a white ostrich feather two feet long was fastened with a single white rose to sweep over the crown and brim. Her bouquet was of white roses.

Miss Gladys Deacon, the bride's elder sister, was her only bridesmaid, or "best girl".
There was no reception afterwards, and the bride and bridegroom left for Paris.

Prince Albert Radziwill is twenty-six years old. He met Miss Dorothy Deacon and her mother at Rome, where they lived for several years. His gifts to his wife include historic family jewels and ropes of pearls of great value. The Palliative Care

Between a good woman who can be relied upon to do her part to maintain the peace and comfort of home life and an honourable man who can be relied upon to provide the material means upon which these depend so much marriage need never be quite a failure. When the charm of sustained personal affection is added marriage should be gloriously happy.
But there is a condition upon which these things largely depend, and that is efficient personal leadership.

Leadership implies superiority. Of any two normally balanced people the senior ought to be mentally and morally superior. It is generally agreed that this superiority is better placed when it falls to the husband. Dual control—and control must enter into life—is as dangerous in marriage.

"Daily Mirror." Reader's £100 Note Sent to the Queen's Brother.
WORK FOR HOSPITAL.

Reading of the illness of the Queen's brother, Prince Francis of Teck, in yesterday's Daily Mirror, and of the splendid efforts that the Prince has been making to complete the collection of £20,000 to free the Middlesex Hospital from debt, a reader of The Daily Mirror telephoned to the Editor yesterday morning to say that he would like to make a donation to the Middlesex Hospital Fund.
Half an hour later this reader handed to The Daily Mirror a Bank of England note for £100, and expressed the hope that the fund would be completed before Prince Francis was out of the doctors' hands.

The donor insists upon complete anonymity. "I give it," he said, "because I so greatly admire the splendid work, the Prince has done for the hospital, and I think there could be no greater aid to his rapid recovery than the completion of the £20,000 that he has set himself to collect.
CLEARING OFF OUTSTANDING SUM.

"But there is another reason. I have been at various times, and still am, a patient at the same nursing home where the Prince is, so that we are in a way fellow-sufferers, and I make my subscription partly out of gratitude for the many kindnesses I have received at that home."
Prince Francis is at Miss Clara Nelson-Smith's Nursing Home at 15, Welbeck-street.
The generous reader explained that he did not wish to be described in any other way than as a patient of Miss Nelson-Smith's home.

"The idea occurred to me in reading your paper this morning," he added, "and, as I have said. I heartily agreed with the opinion expressed there, that could the comparatively small sum still outstanding be raised before the Prince leaves his sick-room it would do much to hasten his recovery."
THE PRINCE DELIGHTED.
Later in the day The Daily Mirror conveyed the 2100 note to the Prince Francis handed it to Mr. F. C. Melhado, the secretary-superintendent, who is carrying on the Prince's work.
Prince Francis was delighted when the news was conveyed to him by the secretary-superintendent.
"If only all Daily Mirror readers were to be as generous in proportion to their means I should not have to suffer from writers' cramp in appealing for funds for the hospital," he said.

The Daily Mirror was informed last night that the Prince was making a satisfactory recovery, and that there was every hope that he would be back at his work in a very short time. (Photograph on page 13.)

EX-ARCHBISHOP
OF YORK DEAD.
A distinguished feature in the Church of England passed away yesterday, Dr. Molean, late Archbishop of York, succumb in attack of pneumonia at the age of eighty days.

He was able to drive in the Park on Sunday week, but on the following day had to take to his bed. He passed away at 15, Queen's Gateplace, Kensington, in the presence of Mrs. Maclagan, his son and daughter, yesterday afternoon.

Archbishop and Many Prelates Take Part in Consecration at Westminster.

With ancient rite and ceremony the Catholic Cathedral of the Most Precious Blood at Westminster, begun forty years ago as a memorial to the life-work of Cardinal Wiseman, the first Archbishop of Westminster, wassecrated yesterday.
Archbishop Bourne was the chief officiating pre-late, and with him were the entire Roman Catholic hierarchy of England. The ceremony began at 7 a.m., and lasted until 2.30 p.m.
First of all, clad in magnificent vestments, the Archbishop-blessed water, cast salt in it, and commenced a circuit of the cathedral outside.
Then, knocking the door with his pastoral staff, he pronounced the words: "Lift up your gates, ye princess, and be ye lifted up, ye everlasting gates, and the King of Gloria shall come in."
"Who is the King oforz?" asked a deacon from inside, and, receiving the reply: "The Lord, strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle," threw open the door.

Ashes were strewn on the floor and the Archbishop traced a cross composed of the letters of the Latin and Greek alphabets arranged saltire-wise. Then the highutar and side altars were concentrated, fourteen prelates being engaged in this.

Meanwhile a large crowd, including among them the Duke of Norfolk, was waiting for the procession of the relics from the Cathedral Hall to the Cathedral. The relics were borne on biers, followed by the Archbishop preceded by fourteen Bishops in gold and crimson and gold and purple metres.
Then the public were admitted for the "burial" of the relics.
Then followed the Mass of Dedication, and at the Elevation of the Host the great bell lately placed in St. Edward's tower peeled for the first time.

Vespers—the first of a series of thanksgiving services for the conseceration of the metropolitan cathedral and for the restoration of the English hierarchy—were sung in the evening, the serum being reached by the Bishop of Clifton.

ASSEMBLING OF RECORD FLEET.
Three Hundred Ships to Take Part in Naval Manoeuvres Early Next Month.
There were scenes of activity at the naval ports yesterday, when the mobilisation of battleships to take part in the manoeuvres, which last for three weeks, began.

It is understood that the squadrons to take part will comprise the Home, Channel and Atlantic Fleets, and will establish a record in the matter of concentrated strength. Some 300 vessels are to assemble at Portland and Torbay early next month.

In all the mobilisation involves the calling up and disposal on shipboard of 17,000 seamen, stokers and marines. The locale of the manoeuvres has not been divulged, but it is probable that the Atlantic will be the scene of the mimic encounter between the rival fleets.

ROLLER-SKATER'S FALL.
London Clerk Sues for Damages for Injury at Brixton Rink.
A roller-skater's fall was the subject of an action claiming damages for injury that came yesterday before Mr. Justice Hamilton and a jury, and was adjourned.
The unfortunate skater was Mr. John Ethelbert Lionel Hayes, a clerk in the London City and Midland Bank.

By Daniel Chaucer, Mr. Chaucer's story describes a colony of people, most of them cranks, who settle down in a village built expressly for them, with the intention, more or less sincere, of leading the simple life. The incidents are described with a real sense of humour, and the introduction of a Russian Anarchist, who understands nothing of what they are all aiming at, adds to the amusement of the reader. The experiment is found to be costly, unprofitable, and even immoral in its results. Everard, the music-hall manager, not himself a "lifer," is the most sympathetic amongst these remarkably well-drawn and distinctive characters. The chief merit of the book is its wit, which provokes many a hrasty laugh. (John Lane, 68.)
